hints: Think about how water bonds to a positive metal ion using a lone pair on oxygen, where both shared electrons come from one atom.
Think about how water can interact with a negative nitrate ion through its slightly positive hydrogen atoms.
walkthrough:
See water bonding to the magnesium ion**
Picture $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ as a small, highly charged positive ion. Each water molecule has two lone pairs on oxygen. The oxygen donates a lone pair into a vacant orbital on $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. Because both electrons in the shared pair come from oxygen, this is a dative covalent bond, also called a coordinate bond. This forms the complex ion $[\text{Mg}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$.

See water bonding to the nitrate ion**
Now look at the other side. Water has $\delta+$ hydrogen atoms and nitrate has $\delta-$ oxygen atoms. The H atom of a coordinated water molecule is attracted to an O atom of $\text{NO}_3^-$. That attraction between H attached to O and a lone pair on another electronegative O is hydrogen bonding.

Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$: dative covalent (coordinate) bonding.
$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$: hydrogen bonding.

hints: Recall the shape formed when six identical ligands arrange to stay as far apart as possible around a central ion.
walkthrough:
Count the ligands and place them symmetrically**
You have six water molecules around one $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. Six bonding pairs repel to maximum separation. That gives four waters in a square plane with one above and one below the plane, all at $90^{\circ}$. This is the octahedral arrangement, the normal shape for $[\text{Mg}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$.
Final answer: Octahedral arrangement of six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules around $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.

hints: Remember gentle heating first drives off water of crystallisation without breaking the nitrate, so look for dissolving and condensation.
Recall the general Group 2 nitrate decomposition to oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen.
Link brown fumes to $\text{NO}_2$ and relighting of a glowing splint to $\text{O}_2$.
Combine the two stages into two balanced equations and select three clear observations including the white solid residue.
walkthrough:
Separate gentle heating from strong heating**
Gentle heating does not decompose nitrate. It simply breaks the dative bonds to water. The crystal dissolves in its own water of crystallisation and water vapour condenses on the cool wall of the tube: $$\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Decompose the anhydrous nitrate strongly**
On stronger heating, the small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion polarises the nitrate ion so strongly that it breaks down. The products for a Group 2 nitrate are always metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: $$\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{MgO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$$ Check balance: Mg 1 to 1, N 2 to 2, O 6 to 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.

Translate each product into what you see**
Water gives colourless liquid condensing near the top. $\text{NO}_2$ gives dense brown fumes. $\text{MgO}$ gives a white solid residue. $\text{O}_2$ is colourless but can be tested with a glowing splint which relights. For full credit describe at least three of these clearly, distinguishing observation from inference.

Final answer: $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
$\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{MgO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$
Observations, any three of: solid dissolves / turns to liquid; condensation / droplets of water on cool part of tube; brown fumes of $\text{NO}_2$ evolved; white solid of $\text{MgO}$ remains; gas evolved that relights a glowing splint ($\text{O}_2$).

hints: Calculate $M_r$ of $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $M_r$ of the final residue $\text{MgO}$ to find the molar mass lost.
Express that loss as a percentage of the starting hydrated mass using $100 \times \text{loss} / \text{initial}$.
walkthrough:
Find the starting and finishing molar masses**
Strong heating to constant mass means all water and all decomposition gases are lost, leaving only $\text{MgO}$. Using atomic masses: $$M_r[\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}] = 24.3 + 2 \times (14.0 + 48.0) + 6 \times 18.0 = 256.3$$ $$M_r[\text{MgO}] = 24.3 + 16.0 = 40.3$$ So molar loss $= 256.3 - 40.3 = 216.0$.

Convert loss to percentage**
Percentage loss is always relative to the starting mass: $$\text{percentage loss} = \frac{216.0}{256.3} \times 100 = 84.3\%$$ This large loss makes sense because six waters plus $2\text{NO}_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$ are all driven off.

hints: Compare the size and charge density of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ at the top with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ at the bottom of Group 2.
Think about how a small highly polarising cation distorts the electron cloud of $\text{NO}_3^-$ and weakens the N to O bond.
walkthrough:
Track ionic size down the group**
All Group 2 ions are 2+, but an extra electron shell is added each step from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. The ionic radius increases, so the same 2+ charge is spread over a larger volume. Charge density and polarising power therefore fall.

Link polarisation to stability**
Decomposition happens because the cation pulls electron density away from the nitrate ion, distorting it and weakening the N-O bond so it breaks to give oxide plus $\text{NO}_2$. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ distorts strongly, so decomposition is easy. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ distorts only weakly, so the nitrate is more stable to heat.

Final answer: Down Group 2 the cationic radius increases / ionic size increases.
The larger cation has lower charge density and polarises / distorts the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion less, so more heat is needed to decompose it.

hints: Use the clue that the gases are the same as for magnesium nitrate ($\text{NO}_2$ + $\text{O}_2$) but the solid is silver metal, not an oxide, then balance.
walkthrough:
Write the products and balance**
Silver is below copper in reactivity, so its oxide is unstable to heat and silver metal forms directly. Keep the familiar gases $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$: $$2\text{AgNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{Ag} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$ Check: Ag 2 to 2, N 2 to 2, O 6 to 4 + 2 = 6. Balanced.
